To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we performed a genome-wide association study (GWA) to identify genes underlying tolerance of hydrolysate toxins in 165 strains of yeast, and found that the genetic architecture of toxin tolerance is highly dependent on strain background.

(1) we identified genetic variants in S. cerevisiae strains that are involved in toxin tolerance, (2) the genes identified as being involved in toxin tolerance are different in different strain backgrounds, (3) the difference in the underlying genes that are involved is a bigger factor in strain-specific differences than allelic differences, and (4) our results raise important considerations for interpreting GWA studies and engineering strategies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
engineering microbes to tolerate toxins that are generated in the process of converting plant biomass to fuels and chemicals.
engineering yeast for the production of biofuels from plant biomass.
engineering microbes for tolerance of toxins that are produced during biomass processing, and we are using natural diversity as a resource to understand the genetic mechanisms of tolerance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the genetic architecture of hydrolysate-tolerance in S. cerevisiae is complex, and that there is substantial variation in the causal genes underlying tolerance, even between two closely related strains.
the genetic architecture of toxin tolerance is highly complex and strain-dependent, and the mechanisms are likely to be different in different strains.
the genetic architecture underlying tolerance of hydrolysate toxins is very strain-dependent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have identified a number of genetic variants underlying toxin-tolerance in S. cerevisiae, and that the underlying gene requirements are very dependent on genetic background.
GWA is a useful approach to identify genetic variants involved in toxin tolerance in yeast.
we found a lot of variation in underlying gene requirement for hydrolysate tolerance, but we did not find any genes that were consistently important across all strains.
The main takeaway from our work is that
genetic architecture of a trait can vary dramatically between strains, and that strain-specific genetic architecture can be a major determinant of the success of engineering efforts.

the genetic architecture of hydrolysate-tolerance mechanisms is very strain-dependent, and that strain background should be considered when interpreting GWA results, as well as when designing engineering strategies to improve tolerance.

GWA studies can uncover important genetic determinants for tolerance to hydrolysate toxins, but the results are strain-dependent, and therefore, the results from one strain may not necessarily be applicable to another strain.
